Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Isaiah 1.

---

## Isaiah 1 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — The Superscription

This verse is the title for the whole book. Isaiah ("the LORD saves" or "salvation of the LORD") was the son of Amoz (not the prophet Amos). He prophesied across four reigns — Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah — spanning from about 740 to 680 B.C. Jewish tradition holds that Amoz was a brother of King Amaziah, making Isaiah of royal blood, though this cannot be proved biblically. The prophecy is called a "vision" because it was perceived by spiritual sight, and the term suggests clarity of divine revelation. Isaiah was a contemporary of Hosea and Micah.

- Enduring Word notes that this chapter was probably delivered during the reign of the wicked king Ahaz (2 Kings 16; 2 Chronicles 28). During this period Judah was repeatedly invaded by surrounding nations. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Gill notes the Jewish tradition that where a prophet's father is named, the father was also a prophet. He also notes that Isaiah began to prophesy about A.M. 3236, roughly 770 years before Christ, and lived to an old age. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/1.htm
- Matthew Henry observes that the prophecy is called a "vision" because it was revealed to Isaiah when awake, and that prophets were called "seers." He suggests (following Calvin) that this first sermon may have been affixed to the temple door for all to read (Hab. 2:2). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/isaiah/1.htm
- Ellicott dates the chapter to the latter part of Jotham's reign, embodying results of Isaiah's study of Uzziah's reign, possibly retouched under Hezekiah. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/1.htm
- Precept Austin notes that the LXX renders the name as "Esaias the son of Amos." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_11-4_commentary

---

### v. 2 — Heaven and Earth Called as Witnesses

God calls heaven and earth as "witnesses" or a "jury" in a covenant lawsuit against His people. The language echoes Deuteronomy 32:1 ("Give ear, O heavens … and let the earth hear"). The charge is that God has "raised children" (or "magnified and exalted" children, as Gill notes) but they have rebelled — a sin aggravated by the parent-child relationship. This is not merely a legal breach but a personal betrayal of a Father's love.

- Enduring Word: Heaven and earth act as a "jury" before which God presents His case. Creation groans under sin (Rom. 8:22) and has an interest in human obedience. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Gill: The Targum paraphrases "they have rebelled against my Word" — i.e., against the essential Word, the Messiah. The word for "nourished" can also mean "magnified" or "exalted." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/1.htm
- Expositor's Bible Commentary (Nicoll): This is a Trial or Assize — "The Great Arraignment" (Ewald). God is at once Plaintiff and Judge; heaven and earth are Assessors. The charge is "brutish, ingrate stupidity, breaking out into rebellion." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/isaiah-1.html
- Precept Austin: Calls this "Jehovah's Indictment of Judah & Jerusalem," with heaven, earth, and even brute beasts as witnesses. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_12-4_commentary

---

### v. 3 — Dumber Than the Beasts

The ox knows its owner; the donkey knows where it is fed. But Israel "does not know" and "does not understand" (or "consider"). This is a searing comparison: even dumb animals recognise their master and source of provision, but God's own covenant people lack this basic recognition. The Hebrew verb for "consider" implies a voluntary, self-stirring act of understanding.

- Enduring Word: Judah was "dumber than dumb animals." No animal has ever offended or rejected God as every human being has. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Gill: The ass knows the "crib" or "manger" where it is fed. Gussetius interprets this as the ass knowing the threshing floor — it goes willingly even to labour because food is there. Israel, by contrast, was weary of temple worship where spiritual food was provided. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/1.htm
- Matthew Henry: "Not considering what we do know in religion, does us as much harm, as ignorance of what we should know." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/isaiah-1.html
- Expositor's Bible Commentary: "They do not think." They are God's grown-up children with reason and conscience developed, but they use neither. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/isaiah-1.html

---

### v. 4 — The Five-Fold Indictment

The prophet piles up descriptions of Judah's sin: "sinful nation," "people laden with iniquity," "brood of evildoers," "children of depravity" (or "children that are corrupters"). The three concluding clauses specify their sin: they have *forsaken* the LORD, *despised* the Holy One of Israel, and *turned their backs* on Him. The title "Holy One of Israel" is a favourite of Isaiah (used about 25 times in the book), emphasizing God's utter separateness from sin.

- Enduring Word: God "clearly and strongly exposed their sin." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Gill: "A people laden with iniquity" — they were "heavy" with sin yet felt no burden. "Children that are corrupters" — they corrupted themselves and others. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/1.htm
- Precept Austin (D.L. Moody): Lists this verse as part of a "tenfold accusation" spanning vv. 2-4. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_1_resources

---

### vv. 5-6 — The Beaten Body

God asks, "Why do you want more beatings?" Despite chastisement, Judah keeps rebelling. The nation is pictured as a body beaten from head to foot — "no soundness," only wounds, welts, and festering sores that have not been cleansed, bandaged, or soothed with oil. The imagery is of a body left untreated, and the point is that further chastisement would be useless because they have not responded to what they have already received.

- Enduring Word: God did not wish evil upon Judah; He longed for them to repent. But they would continue to be stricken as long as they rebelled. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Gill: The "head" represents civil rulers; the "heart" represents priests. Both were corrupted. Alternatively, the whole body politic was afflicted without reformation. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/1.htm
- Precept Austin: "God's rod of chastisement has not succeeded, even though their body is covered with wounds and bruises! Brute beasts are more responsive than Judah." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_15-9_commentary
- Ellicott notes Isaiah may have had medical training (see also Isa. 38:21), reflected in his precise description of untreated wounds. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/1.htm

---

### vv. 7-8 — The Desolate Land and the Lonely City

The land is desolate, cities burned, fields devoured by foreigners while the people watch helplessly. "Daughter of Zion" (a tender personification of Jerusalem) is left as isolated as a temporary shelter in a vineyard or a hut in a cucumber field — structures occupied only in harvest season and then abandoned. Jerusalem stands alone like a city under siege.

- Enduring Word: During Ahaz's reign, Judah was attacked by Israel, Syria, Edom, the Philistines, and Assyria (2 Chr. 28). "For the LORD brought Judah low because of Ahaz" (2 Chr. 28:19). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Precept Austin: The shelter/hut imagery emphasizes total abandonment — "a vineyard without fruit, the cottage alone indicating that it was a vineyard." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_15-9_commentary
- Gray's Concise Bible Commentary: The "cottage" was the shelter of the vineyard keeper; but Judah's desolation represented a vineyard without fruit — Jerusalem was "about all that remained to her at this time." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/isaiah-1.html

---

### v. 9 — The Remnant Preserved

Unless the LORD of Hosts had left a "few survivors" (a remnant), Judah would have been totally annihilated like Sodom and Gomorrah. This is both an acknowledgment of mercy and a warning: morally, Judah is on Sodom's level. The remnant theme is central to Isaiah's theology. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 9:29 to show that God's sovereign preservation of a remnant is an act of grace.

- Enduring Word: As bad as things were, it was only God's mercy that they survived at all. Sodom and Gomorrah were totally destroyed with no remnant. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Matthew Henry: God's grace and goodness in reserving a few kept them from becoming like Sodom. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/isaiah/1.htm
- Precept Austin entitles this section: "Remnant That Prevents Destruction." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_11-4_commentary

---

### v. 10 — Rulers of Sodom, People of Gomorrah

God addresses Judah's leaders as "rulers of Sodom" and the populace as "people of Gomorrah." This is a shocking rhetorical strategy — He is not speaking to literal Sodomites but to Israelites whose behaviour mirrors those infamous cities. He calls them to hear the "law" (torah, instruction) of God, implying they have abandoned not just ritual but God's moral teaching.

- Enduring Word: God associated Judah with the two cities most synonymous with sin and judgment to get their attention. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Gill: Both rulers and people are called under those names to hearken to the law of God and not trust in sacrifices and ceremonies. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/1.htm
- Gray's Concise Commentary: "The names Sodom and Gomorrah are used metaphorically." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/isaiah-1.html

---

### vv. 11-15 — Empty Worship Rejected

This passage is the classic Old Testament rejection of hypocritical worship. God asks what good their "multitude of sacrifices" does Him. He is "full" (sated, as with food) from burnt offerings; He takes "no delight" in blood. He calls their temple attendance "trampling of My courts." Their incense is "detestable" (an abomination). Even the divinely appointed observances — New Moons, Sabbaths, convocations — God "hates" and finds a "burden." When they spread their hands in prayer, He will hide His eyes and refuse to listen. The reason: "Your hands are covered with blood."

**Key point**: God is not rejecting the sacrificial system He ordained; He is rejecting worship offered by unrepentant hearts and blood-stained hands. The problem is the combination of "iniquity and the sacred meeting" (v. 13).

- Enduring Word: God's reaction is described with strong language: "I have had enough … an abomination … I cannot endure … My soul hates … I am weary." Without the right heart, God hated their religious ceremony and service. David Guzik notes that when sinners are under judgment, they "will more easily be brought to fly to their devotions than to forsake their sins" (quoting Matthew Henry). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Gill: They were not to trust in sacrifices and rites of the ceremonial law along with hypocritical prayers; these were abominable because of their dreadful immoralities. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/1.htm
- Matthew Henry: "It is plain that the sacrifices of the law could not atone, even for outward national crimes." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/isaiah-1.html
- Expositor's Bible Commentary: "In all their worship conscience is asleep, and they are drenched in wickedness. Isaiah puts their life in an epigram — Wickedness and worship: 'I cannot away,' saith the Lord, 'with wickedness and worship.'" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/isaiah-1.html
- Precept Austin entitles this section: "Religion That Sickens God." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_11-4_commentary

---

### vv. 16-17 — The Call to Repentance and Social Justice

The command is: "Wash and cleanse yourselves. Remove your evil deeds … Stop doing evil! Learn to do right; seek justice and correct the oppressor. Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow." Repentance is not only turning from evil but actively pursuing good — particularly justice for the vulnerable. The orphan and widow represent those without a human protector in ancient society.

- Enduring Word: The corruption was shown in their bad treatment of one another. John later repeated this message: "If someone says, 'I love God,' and hates his brother, he is a liar" (1 John 4:20). God cared more about how they treated the weak than about their ceremonies. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Precept Austin (D.L. Moody): Lists this as an "eight-fold instruction." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_1_resources
- Expositor's Bible Commentary: "Forgiveness is no end in itself, but the opportunity of social service; not a sanctuary … but a gateway through which he leads God's people upon the world." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/isaiah-1.html

---

### v. 18 — "Come Now, Let Us Reason Together"

This is one of the most beloved verses in Isaiah. God invites His people to settle the dispute. The phrase has been translated "let us reason together" (KJV) or "let us settle the matter" (NIV). The Expositor's Bible Commentary, following Cheyne, translates it "let us bring our reasoning to an end" — the conclusion of the lawsuit, not the beginning of debate.

The promise is that scarlet and crimson sins — dyes that were considered colourfast, impossible to wash out — will become white as snow and as wool. This points to a supernatural cleansing.

- Enduring Word: Following God is "the most reasonable thing we can do." The cleansing is accomplished through Christ's work, not through good works, suffering, or time. Spurgeon is quoted at length: "The Lord does not deny the truth of what the sinner has confessed … 'Though your sins be as scarlet, I meet you on that ground.'" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Gill: The exhortation is to "repentance for sin, to the obedience of faith, and washing in the blood of Christ, whereby their crimson and scarlet sins would become as white as wool and snow." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/1.htm
- Matthew Henry: "Though our sins have been as scarlet and crimson, a deep dye, a double dye, first in the wool of original corruption, and afterwards in the many threads of actual transgression … yet pardoning mercy will take out the stain." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/isaiah-1.html
- Expositor's Bible Commentary: "So plain an offer of pardon is not reasoning together; it is bringing reasoning to an end; it is the settlement of a dispute that has been in progress." Only the Bible can combine God's pardon with His reproach in a single verse. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/isaiah-1.html
- Precept Austin (D.L. Moody): "No matter how fast the color is, the blood of Jesus Christ can wash it out." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_1_resources

---

### vv. 19-20 — The Choice: Blessing or the Sword

God sets before Judah the two ways: "If you are willing and obedient, you will eat the best of the land. But if you resist and rebel, you will be devoured by the sword." The closing formula, "For the mouth of the LORD has spoken," stamps the choice with divine authority. This is covenant language: blessing for obedience, curse for rebellion (cf. Deuteronomy 28).

- Enduring Word: "No one perfectly matches either phrase, but which phrase better describes your life? … There is a consequence for either course: eat of the good of the land or be devoured by the sword." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Matthew Henry: "Life and death, good and evil, are set before us." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/isaiah-1.html

---

### vv. 21-23 — The Faithful City Became a Harlot

Jerusalem, once "full of justice" and "righteousness," has become a harlot — spiritual adultery through idolatry and unfaithfulness. Now it harbours murderers. The silver has become dross (worthless impurity), the wine diluted with water. The rulers are rebels, "friends of thieves," loving bribes, chasing rewards. They do not defend the fatherless, and the widow's plea never reaches them. This is a comprehensive indictment of leadership failure.

- Enduring Word: "The faithful city has become a harlot" — spiritually, they have forsaken their "marriage" to the LORD. Silver-to-dross and wine-to-water are images of debasement and dilution. Guzik quotes Bultema: "The Lord Jesus made water into wine; sinners make wine into water." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Gill: A lamentation over the deplorable state of Jerusalem — the difference between what it was and what it had become, and the degeneracy of rulers and judges. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/1.htm
- Matthew Henry: "Dross may shine like silver, and the wine that is mixed with water may still have the colour of wine." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/isaiah-1.html

---

### vv. 24-26 — God Will Purge and Restore

The Lord GOD of Hosts, the "Mighty One of Israel," announces that He will be "relieved of My foes" and "avenge Myself on My enemies." Remarkably, He then says, "I will turn My hand against you" — the very people of Judah are His enemies because of their sin. Yet the purpose is purifying, not merely punitive: "I will thoroughly purge your dross; I will remove all your impurities." The metallurgical image is of a refiner removing alloy from precious metal. Then God promises restoration: judges and counsellors "as at the first … as at the beginning," and Jerusalem will again be called "the City of Righteousness, the Faithful City."

- Enduring Word: "God's redemption always comes with justice and righteousness — He never saves at the expense of His own character." The purification is like a metalsmith refining ore. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Gill: The Lord foretells what He will do — avenge Himself of enemies, purge His church and people, restore them to uprightness, and redeem them. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/1.htm
- Gray's Concise Commentary: The period of judgment runs "throughout the history of Judah down to the end of this age." vv. 26-27 "speak of a time not yet realized in her experience." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/isaiah-1.html
- Matthew Henry applies this to (1) Hezekiah's reformation, (2) return from Babylon, (3) the gospel kingdom and New Testament church as "a new Jerusalem, a city of righteousness," and (4) the second coming of Christ. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/isaiah/1.htm

---

### v. 27 — Redemption for the Repentant

"Zion will be redeemed with justice, her repentant ones with righteousness." Redemption (being bought back) and righteousness are linked. Only those who repent share in the redemption. God's justice, which seemed to stand against Zion in judgment, now becomes the instrument of her salvation.

- Enduring Word: God's redemption always comes with justice and righteousness. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Matthew Henry: "The redemption of the spiritual Zion, by the righteousness and death of Christ, and by his powerful grace, most fully accord with what is here meant. Sin is the worst captivity, the worst slavery." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/isaiah-1.html
- Gray's Concise Commentary: This will be fulfilled when "Zion, or the kingdom of Judah, shall have been redeemed with judgment." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/isaiah-1.html

---

### v. 28 — Destruction for Rebels and Sinners

In sharp contrast to the repentant who are redeemed, "rebels and sinners will together be shattered, and those who forsake the LORD will perish." There is no middle ground: the choice presented in vv. 19-20 leads to two irreconcilable destinies.

- Gill: A denunciation of utter destruction upon wicked men, described as idolaters. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/1.htm

---

### vv. 29-31 — Shame, Withering, and Unquenchable Fire

Those who delighted in "sacred oaks" and chose "gardens" — references to idolatrous pagan worship sites (Canaanite fertility cults often involved sacred trees and garden shrines) — will be ashamed. They will become like a withered oak or a garden without water. The "strong man" (or the idol, depending on interpretation) will become tinder (literally "tow," fibres of flax easily ignited), his work a spark; both will burn together with no one to quench the flames.

- Enduring Word: The "sacred oaks" (terebinth trees) and "gardens" were sites of idol worship. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Gill: The destruction is illustrated "by the fading of the leaves of an oak, and by a garden parched with drought … and it is suggested that it will be by burning with fire unquenchable." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/1.htm
- Matthew Henry: "Even the strong man shall be as tow; not only soon broken, and pulled to pieces, but easily catching fire. When the sinner has made himself as tow and stubble, and God makes himself as a consuming fire, what can prevent the utter ruin of the sinner?" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/isaiah-1.html

---

## Points of Differing Emphasis Among Traditions

**Baptist/Reformed emphasis on total depravity and sovereign grace (seen especially in v. 9 "remnant" and v. 18):**
- Enduring Word (broadly evangelical/Pentecostal-leaning but citing Spurgeon) stresses that cleansing in v. 18 is entirely through Christ's work, not through good works, suffering, or time. The remnant in v. 9 is preserved purely by God's mercy. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-1/
- Gill (Reformed Baptist) explicitly interprets v. 18 as pointing to "washing in the blood of Christ." He reads v. 9's remnant through the lens of sovereign election. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/1.htm

**Wesleyan/Methodist emphasis on the moral response and social holiness (vv. 16-17):**
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary (broadly Protestant but with strong social conscience themes) stresses that forgiveness is "not a sanctuary … but a gateway" to social action — "Seek justice, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow." Conscience drives the forgiven person outward into the world. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/isaiah-1.html
- The call to "cease to do evil, learn to do good" (vv. 16-17) is interpreted as evidence that true repentance must bear social fruit — a hallmark of Wesleyan social holiness.

**Matthew Henry (Puritan/Reformed Anglican) — multi-layered fulfilment:**
- Henry sees multiple fulfilments for the promises of vv. 24-27: Hezekiah's reformation, return from Babylon, the gospel age, and the second coming of Christ — a classic covenantal/dispensational blending. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/isaiah/1.htm

**The "reason together" translation debate (v. 18):**
- The traditional rendering "let us reason together" (KJV, followed by Enduring Word and many evangelical commentaries) suggests a rational dialogue. The Expositor's Bible Commentary (Nicoll, following Cheyne) argues the Hebrew means "let us bring our reasoning to an end" — the conclusion of the lawsuit, not the start of a debate. This affects whether one sees the verse as an invitation to rational argument or a declaration that the dispute is settled by God's offer of pardon. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/isaiah-1.html

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship — Date and Occasion:**
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary notes that the chapter was likely published late in Isaiah's life. The invasion described in v. 7 best fits Sennacherib's campaign of 701 B.C. (though some scholars propose Sargon's invasion of 711 or the Syro-Ephraimite crisis of 734). The chapter was "lifted out of its original circumstance and placed in the front of the book … as a general introduction." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/isaiah-1.html

**Catholic Reading:**
- Unable to fetch specific Catholic commentary pages. However, the traditional Catholic reading (reflected in the Vulgate and patristic sources) generally aligns with the historic interpretation: Isaiah 1 is a call to interior conversion rather than mere external ritual — a major theme echoed in the Church's teaching on sacraments being validly received only with proper disposition. The "wash and cleanse" language of v. 16 has traditionally been read in light of baptismal regeneration. (Specific page could not be accessed within limits.)

**Orthodox Reading:**
- Unable to access oca.org content within limits. Orthodox tradition, following the Septuagint, reads Isaiah 1 as a call to purification of the heart and to true noetic prayer over empty ritual. The "reason together" of v. 18 in the LXX is rendered with a term suggesting dialogue and disputation, understood in the Greek fathers as God condescending to dialogue with humanity.
